title: THE APOSTLES HAD THE POWER OF GOD. TODAY’S FALSE APOSTLES WANT THE POWER OVER YOU.
paragraphs: THE APOSTLES HAD THE POWER OF GOD. TODAY’S FALSE APOSTLES WANT THE POWER OVER YOU.

Acts 2:42–43 reveals what genuine apostolic authority looked like. And the difference between the first-century Church and some of today's self-appointed spiritual authorities should make every Christian open their Bible again.

There is something deeply disturbing about a man standing behind a pulpit, demanding that people recognize his apostolic authority, while the very Scripture he uses to defend himself exposes everything wrong with his ministry.
He quotes Acts 2.
He speaks about signs and wonders.
He reminds everyone that God appointed apostles to lead His Church.
And somewhere in the congregation sits a struggling mother who has barely enough money to feed her children, wondering whether refusing to give another offering means she is resisting God.
A young believer is afraid to ask questions because he has been taught that questioning the apostle is rebellion.
A wounded Christian has watched leaders escape accountability while ordinary members are publicly humiliated for much smaller failures.
And someone who genuinely loves Jesus is beginning to wonder whether following Christ means surrendering their conscience to a man who claims to speak for Him.
But here is the question that changes everything.
When Luke wrote Acts 2:42–43, was he describing men who demanded unquestioning loyalty, financial privilege, and spiritual superiority? Or was he describing something entirely different?
Because if we misunderstand these two verses, we may mistake religious control for spiritual authority.
And if we understand them correctly, we may finally recognize the difference between shepherds who serve Christ and wolves who use His name.
Listen carefully.
The greatest danger is not always someone openly denying Jesus.
Sometimes it is someone speaking constantly about Jesus while quietly placing himself where only Jesus belongs.
And Acts 2:42–43 gives us a remarkable place to begin examining that danger.
The King James Version records:
“And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles.”
— Acts 2:42–43, KJV
At first glance, these verses appear simple.
The believers followed the apostles' teaching. They lived in fellowship. They broke bread. They prayed. God worked signs and wonders through the apostles.
But underneath those familiar words is a truth that challenges both religious deception and our own tendency to put human personalities on pedestals.
The early Church was not built around the celebrity of the apostles.
It was built around the risen Jesus Christ whom the apostles proclaimed.
That distinction is everything.
Look at the original Greek of Acts 2:42.
“Ἦσαν δὲ προσκαρτεροῦντες τῇ διδαχῇ τῶν ἀποστόλων”
Ēsan de proskarterountes tē didachē tōn apostolōn.
A faithful rendering is:
“And they were devoting themselves to the teaching of the apostles.”
The word προσκαρτεροῦντες (proskarterountes) communicates steadfast devotion, perseverance, and continued commitment.
These believers were not casually listening to religious speeches whenever they felt inspired.
They were devoted to the teaching handed down by the apostles.
But notice what the verse actually says.
It does not say they devoted themselves to the apostles' personal ambitions.
It does not say they surrendered their ability to discern truth.
It does not say they were required to finance luxurious lifestyles.
And it certainly does not say that anyone claiming the title of apostle automatically deserves unquestioning obedience.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching.
And what was the center of that teaching?
Jesus Christ.
Just before these verses, Peter had stood before the crowd at Pentecost and proclaimed Jesus' death, resurrection, exaltation, and lordship.
He declared:
“Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.”
— Acts 2:36, KJV
Peter did not stand before the people announcing, “God has made me your supreme spiritual authority. Submit to me.”
He announced Jesus.
The crucified Jesus.
The resurrected Jesus.
The exalted Jesus.
The Jesus whom sinners had rejected, but whom God had vindicated.
And when the people were pierced to the heart and asked what they should do, Peter did not tell them to purchase a blessing or prove their loyalty through financial sacrifice to his ministry.
He told them:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins...”
— Acts 2:38, KJV
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Jesus Christ.
The gift of the Holy Spirit.
That was the message surrounding the birth of the Church.
And it raises an uncomfortable question.
If the apostles' ministry was centered on bringing sinners to Jesus, why do some modern ministries seem centered on bringing believers into permanent dependence upon their leaders?
There is a difference between honoring spiritual leadership and giving a human being authority that belongs to God alone.
There is a difference between receiving biblical correction and being spiritually intimidated.
There is a difference between supporting Gospel ministry and being manipulated into believing that God's love, favor, or blessing is for sale.
And if you have ever been wounded by someone who claimed to represent Jesus, you need to hear this.
A leader's misuse of Scripture does not make Scripture false. And a leader's betrayal of Christ does not make Christ unfaithful.
Now look at the next verse.
Acts 2:43 begins:
“ἐγίνετο δὲ πάσῃ ψυχῇ φόβος”
Egineto de pasē psychē phobos.
A natural translation is:
“And awe was coming upon every soul.”
The Greek word φόβος (phobos) can refer to fear, reverence, or awe, depending on context.
Here, the surrounding description of God's extraordinary activity gives the word a strong sense of reverent awe.
The people were witnessing something beyond ordinary human achievement.
God was working among them.
But notice what Luke does not say.
He does not say the apostles terrified the congregation into submission.
He does not say the believers were afraid to question their leaders.
He does not say spiritual authority was measured by how effectively a minister could intimidate people.
The awe arose in the context of God's work.
And the second half of the verse says:
“πολλά τε τέρατα καὶ σημεῖα διὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐγίνετο”
Polla te terata kai sēmeia dia tōn apostolōn egineto.
“And many wonders and signs were taking place through the apostles.”
Pay attention to one small Greek word.
διά (dia).
In this construction, it means “through.”
The wonders and signs were happening through the apostles.
They were instruments, not the ultimate source.
God was the One at work.
This is consistent with Acts 3, where Peter and John encounter a man who had been unable to walk.
After the man is healed, the crowd looks at the apostles in astonishment.
Peter immediately redirects their attention:
“Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?”
— Acts 3:12, KJV
Read that again.
Peter refuses to take credit for the miracle.
He refuses to let the crowd believe that the healing came from his personal greatness.
He refuses to become the center of the story.
He points them to Jesus.
Now imagine how different some religious platforms would look if every leader responded to admiration the way Peter did.
Imagine a minister refusing to make himself indispensable.
Imagine someone praying for the sick without turning their desperation into a fundraising opportunity.
Imagine a leader who was more concerned about people knowing Christ than people knowing his title.
That is not weakness.
That is a servant understanding who the Master is.
And this brings us to the question many Christians are afraid to ask.
Are the apostles in Acts 2:42–43 the same as the people today who claim apostolic authority?
The direct historical answer is no.
Luke was describing the actual apostles ministering in the earliest Jerusalem Church after Pentecost.
These were identifiable people within a particular moment of redemptive history, including the apostles whom Jesus had chosen and commissioned.
The passage is not a blanket endorsement of everyone throughout history who adopts the title “apostle.”
But we must be careful here.
The Greek word ἀπόστολος (apostolos) broadly means a messenger or one who is sent.
The New Testament uses the term in more than one context.

The Twelve held a foundational and distinctive place in Jesus' ministry. Paul also identified himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, called by God and a witness of the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8–9; Galatians 1:1).
Other passages use apostolic language for individuals serving in particular missionary or representative capacities.
Christians today disagree about whether an apostolic ministry or office continues and, if so, in what sense.
Some believe the foundational apostolic office ended with the first generation of authoritative witnesses to the risen Christ.
Others believe certain apostolic functions, particularly church planting, missionary leadership, and oversight, continue under the authority of Scripture.
Those differences deserve careful biblical discussion.
But one truth does not depend on which position you hold.
No modern claim to apostolic authority gives a person permission to contradict the Gospel, escape accountability, exploit believers, or place himself above the Word of God.
Not one.
And Scripture does not leave us defenseless.
In 2 Corinthians 11:13, Paul writes:
The Greek phrase is striking:
“ψευδαπόστολοι, ἐργάται δόλιοι”
Pseudapostoloi, ergatai dolioi.
“False apostles, deceitful workers.”
Paul was not warning the Church only about people who openly rejected Christianity.
He was warning about people who presented themselves as representatives of Christ while operating deceptively.
That means a title is not proof.
A platform is not proof.
A large congregation is not proof.
A dramatic testimony is not proof.
Even a claim to supernatural power is not sufficient proof.
Jesus Himself warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that some would appeal to prophecy, exorcisms, and mighty works done in His name, yet hear Him reject their claims to belong to Him.
The point is not that every reported miracle is false.
The point is that impressive religious activity cannot replace genuine submission to Christ.
Deuteronomy 13:1–3 had already established that even an apparently extraordinary sign could not justify leading God's people away from Him.
And in the New Testament, believers are explicitly told to test spiritual claims.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.”
— 1 John 4:1, KJV
Notice what Scripture commands.
Test.
Discern.
Examine.
That is not rebellion against God.
That is obedience to God.
And the risen Jesus commended the church at Ephesus because they had tested those who claimed to be apostles and had found some of them false (Revelation 2:2).
Think about that.
Jesus did not condemn them for examining apostolic claims.
He praised their discernment.
So when someone tells you that questioning his doctrine is equivalent to questioning God, remember the words of Christ.
When someone claims that his title places him beyond correction, remember the apostles who themselves taught the Church to test claims.
And when someone insists that genuine submission means silence in the face of wrongdoing, remember that the New Testament never makes a minister's reputation more sacred than the truth.
But there is another side to this conversation that we must not ignore.
Not every leader who makes a mistake is a wolf.
Not every pastor who receives financial support is corrupt.
Not every church that believes spiritual gifts continue is deceptive.
And not everyone who uses the word “apostle” is automatically a false teacher.
Careless accusations can destroy reputations, divide churches, and wound innocent people.
Scripture requires discernment, not suspicion without evidence.

Paul instructed Timothy not to receive an accusation against an elder except on the testimony of two or three witnesses, while also requiring appropriate public rebuke when established sin persisted (1 Timothy 5:19–20).
Truth matters.
Evidence matters.
Justice matters.
And the same Bible that warns us about false leaders also commands us to honor faithful ones.
The question is not simply what someone calls himself.
The question is whether his teaching, conduct, and use of authority withstand biblical examination.
Does he proclaim the biblical Jesus?
Does he faithfully teach the Gospel of grace?
Does he welcome accountability?
Does he demonstrate humility?
Does he handle money honestly?
Does he protect the vulnerable?
Does he serve the flock rather than use the flock to serve himself?
Does he point people toward Christ or make them dependent on his personal approval?
Jesus gave us an unforgettable picture of spiritual leadership in Mark 10:42–45.
The rulers of the nations exercise power over others.
But Jesus tells His disciples that greatness among them must look different.
The great must become servants.
The first must become the servant of all.
And then Jesus points to Himself.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
— Mark 10:45, KJV
There it is.
The pattern.
The standard.
The King of glory did not come to exploit His people.
He came to give His life for them.
How can anyone claim the authority of Christ while despising the servant-hearted character of Christ?
How can a leader demand sacrifices from struggling believers while refusing to sacrifice his own pride?
How can someone preach about the cross while treating ministry as a throne?
The apostle Peter later wrote to church elders:
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.”
— 1 Peter 5:3, KJV
The original Greek includes the expression:
“μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων”
Mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn.
The verb κατακυριεύω (katakyrieuō) conveys the idea of exercising mastery or domineering over others.
Peter explicitly forbids that kind of leadership over God's people.
The same Peter associated with the apostles in Acts 2 later warned elders not to dominate the flock.
That should settle at least one thing.
Apostolic authority was never a license for spiritual tyranny.
And the wider context of Acts 2 makes this even clearer.
Continue reading beyond verse 43.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to people's needs.
The passage is not describing apostles accumulating wealth through pressure while the congregation suffers.
It describes a community marked by generosity and practical care.
Acts 4:34–35 further describes gifts being distributed according to need.
And in Acts 5:4, Peter acknowledges that property belonged to its owner before it was sold and that the proceeds remained under the owner's authority.
The early believers' generosity was real.
But Scripture does not present it as a system in which religious leaders owned the consciences and possessions of everyone in the congregation.
This matters because financial manipulation often hides behind biblical language.
Someone may tell you that if you truly honor God, you must give a particular amount to a particular leader.
Someone may imply that refusing an offering means rejecting a blessing.
Someone may even use the language of tithes, firstfruits, and sacrifice to make you feel that your financial hardship is proof of spiritual failure.
But listen to Paul.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης means “not out of sorrow or compulsion.”
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through fear.
The New Testament does teach that those who minister the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).
Faithful ministry requires resources, and supporting it can be a meaningful act of worship and partnership.
Your obedience to Jesus cannot be reduced to a payment.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
And God's grace is not a premium membership.
That is precisely why any Christian ministry asking for support must be willing to say something that manipulative leaders rarely say:
If you cannot afford to give, you are not less loved by God.
The widow who gave two small coins in Mark 12:41–44 reminds us that Jesus sees the heart and the sacrifice behind a gift, not merely its monetary value.
And Christians must also remember that Scripture calls us to care responsibly for those entrusted to us, especially our households (1 Timothy 5:8).
No faithful ministry should use guilt to force a family to neglect essential needs.
That truth does not weaken Gospel generosity.
It protects it.
Because giving becomes beautiful when love, gratitude, freedom, and sound judgment replace fear.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have never encountered a self-appointed apostle.
Maybe you have never been pressured into giving money.
Maybe your pastor is a humble servant who loves the Scriptures and faithfully cares for the congregation.
Thank God for such leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support them as you are able.
But perhaps your story is different.
Perhaps you once trusted someone who spoke about Jesus with such confidence that you assumed every word he said carried divine authority.
You believed him.
You defended him.
You brought your family to his church.
You gave sacrificially.
You volunteered.
You ignored warning signs because you thought loyalty was the same as faithfulness.
Then something happened.
A question was punished.
A financial irregularity was dismissed.
A wounded person was silenced.
A leader's wrongdoing was covered with spiritual language.
And suddenly, the place where you expected to encounter God's care became a place where you felt afraid.
You began to wonder whether you had failed God.
Maybe you even stopped praying.
Not because you stopped longing for Jesus.
But because someone had made it difficult for you to separate the voice of Christ from the voice of the person who claimed to represent Him.
If that is your story, hear what Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
The Greek is beautifully direct:
“Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός”
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
Jesus is not merely another shepherd competing for your loyalty.
He is the Good Shepherd.
The One whose goodness exposes the failures of every unfaithful shepherd.
The One who knows His sheep.
The One who laid down His life for them.
The One who rose again.
The One whose voice must never be replaced by the voice of a religious personality.
And if you have been harmed by spiritual abuse, returning to Christ does not require returning to an unsafe environment.
Forgiveness does not mean denying wrongdoing.
Grace does not eliminate accountability.
And reconciliation, where appropriate, requires truth and repentance; it cannot be demanded as a substitute for safety.
You can love Jesus while recognizing that someone who claimed to serve Him acted wickedly.
You can honor Scripture while refusing its misuse.
You can seek fellowship with faithful believers without surrendering your conscience to an unaccountable leader.
Because your faith was never supposed to rest on the perfection of a pastor.
It rests on the finished work of Jesus Christ.
But before we point our fingers at every false apostle, there is another question we need to face.
What if the problem is not only the people who demand spiritual celebrity?
What if it is also our willingness to give it to them?
We live in a world fascinated by influence.
We measure importance by followers.
We confuse visibility with faithfulness.
We assume that a large audience means divine approval.
And sometimes we become so impressed by powerful personalities that we stop opening our Bibles for ourselves.
We want someone to tell us what God is saying.
Someone to guarantee our breakthrough.
Someone to promise us success.
Someone to make our faith feel certain without requiring the patient work of knowing Christ through His Word.
But the believers in Berea were commended because they received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to see whether Paul's teaching was true (Acts 17:11).
Think about that.
They examined even Paul's preaching against the Scriptures.
Their discernment did not make them enemies of the Gospel.
It made them noble-minded hearers.
The Church does not need less biblical discernment.
It needs more.
We need believers who can recognize the difference between biblical authority and authoritarian control.
Between spiritual gifts and spiritual showmanship.
Between legitimate financial support and financial exploitation.
Between correction that restores and humiliation that crushes.
Between a leader who points to the cross and a leader who uses the cross as a backdrop for his own glory.
And above all, we need to recover the message that made the apostles' ministry truly powerful.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ reigns as Lord.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy, forgiveness, and new life.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not the greatness of an apostle.
Not the size of a ministry.
Not the spectacle of a platform.
Not the amount of an offering.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose victorious over death.
And the One who is still transforming lives today.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is so deeply personal:
Because the Gospel does not pretend that scandal is harmless.
It does not excuse deception.
It does not rename exploitation as ministry.
It exposes sin, calls sinners to repentance, and announces forgiveness and transformation through Jesus Christ.
The scandal of human pride meets the grace of the humble Savior.
The scandal of betrayal meets the faithfulness of Christ.
The scandal of religious hypocrisy meets the holiness of the One who cannot lie.
And the brokenhearted discover that their story does not have to end where another person's sin left them.
Jesus rewrites lives.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
But by redeeming sinners, restoring hope, and leading His people into truth.
So where does Acts 2:42–43 leave us?
It leaves us looking at a Church devoted to apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer.
It leaves us witnessing God's extraordinary work through the apostles.
It leaves us with a picture of reverence directed toward God rather than manufactured fear of human leaders.
And it leaves us with a standard by which every claim to spiritual authority must be examined.
The passage describes the apostles of the early Church.
It does not automatically validate modern claimants to the apostolic title.
And it certainly does not authorize anyone to manipulate, intimidate, or exploit the people for whom Christ died.
But it also reminds us not to become so consumed with exposing false teachers that we forget to become faithful disciples.
After all, the believers in Acts 2 were not merely identifying what was wrong.
They were devoting themselves to what was right.
The Word.
Fellowship.
Prayer.
Generosity.
Worship.
Life together under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps that is the challenge we need most.
Not simply to ask whether a preacher is genuine.
But to ask whether we ourselves are genuinely following Jesus.
Are we opening Scripture?
Are we growing in repentance?
Are we loving other believers?
Are we caring for those in need?
Are we willing to receive correction from God's Word?
Are we worshiping Christ or merely admiring the people who talk about Him?
Because it is possible to recognize a false apostle and still neglect the true Savior.
And it is possible to win an argument about church authority while losing the tenderness, humility, and love that should characterize a disciple of Jesus.
Don't let that happen.
Let discernment lead you deeper into Scripture.
Let truth lead you toward holiness.
Let your wounds lead you to the Good Shepherd, not away from Him.
And let your love for Christ become visible in how you live, serve, give, and care for others.
You do not have to disclose private details or identify anyone publicly.
Maybe your honest response is simply:
“Jesus, teach me to follow Your voice.”
Or perhaps:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Maybe you have been struggling to trust again, and the words you need to write are:
And if you have witnessed faithful pastors who genuinely reflect the humility of Jesus, share that testimony too.
The Church needs to hear about godly shepherds as well as warnings about false ones.
Your testimony might remind a wounded believer that faithful leadership still exists.
And your prayer might become the beginning of a meaningful conversation with someone who needs the hope of Christ.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with care and kindness, especially if this message could encourage them rather than embarrass them.
You never know who may be quietly struggling with questions they have been afraid to ask.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually complacent, sincere seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus.
Not everyone who reads will agree with every theological conclusion.
That is all right.
Our invitation is to open the Bible, examine the evidence, and keep Jesus Christ at the center.
And if this message has strengthened you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond simply reading another article.
Not because you owe us a tithe.
Not because your commitment to Christ can be measured by a monthly payment.
But because meaningful Gospel ministry takes real work, resources, time, and sustained support.
Not everyone can write articles, develop resources, or dedicate hours to digital discipleship.
But those who believe in the mission can help sustain it.
And that partnership matters.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply one way we hope to thank those who choose to stand with the ministry.
The goal is not merely to gain readers.
It is to encourage disciples.
People who know the Gospel.
People who can recognize deception.
People who grow in holiness and compassion.
People who love Scripture more than spiritual spectacle.
People who follow Jesus even when following Him is costly.
Your value to God is not determined by your financial contribution to Gospel Warrior.
Christ is the Savior.
We are servants.
And that order must never be reversed.
That is what makes this mission worth supporting.
Not a demand for unquestioning loyalty.
Not a promise that money will purchase blessings.
But an invitation to participate freely in making Christ known.
Before you leave, return with me to that first gathering of believers in Jerusalem.
Imagine the prayers.
The fellowship.
The bread being broken.
The Scriptures being taught.
The astonishment as God worked among His people.
Imagine Peter standing before a crowd and refusing to take credit for what Jesus had done.
Imagine a community learning that greatness in the Kingdom of God does not look like domination.
It looks like service.
It looks like truth.
It looks like generosity.
It looks like love.
And above all, it looks like the crucified and risen Christ.
That is the Church we should long to become.
Not a people captivated by titles.
Not a people terrified of human personalities.
Not a people who mistake religious performance for spiritual life.
But a people so rooted in Jesus that deception loses its power over them.
Because one day, every platform will be silent.
Every earthly title will fade.
Every reputation will be weighed before the perfect judgment of God.
And the question that matters most will not be whether we followed the most impressive religious personality.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
So test the teaching.
Honor faithful shepherds.
Reject spiritual exploitation.
Repent of your own sins.
Extend grace without abandoning truth.
And never surrender to a human leader the worship, trust, and ultimate allegiance that belong to Jesus alone.
The hands that were pierced for your salvation will never need a counterfeit apostle to hold your soul hostage.
